analysis.one_liner: Bans the manufacture, use, and sale of asbestos, with a two-year exception for chlorine plants.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 37 cosponsors but never got a hearing, markup, or vote; it died in a House Energy and Commerce subcommittee before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the nation's main toxics law to ban making, processing, using, and selling commercial asbestos and products containing it, one year after enactment. Existing chlorine plants would get a two-year window to keep importing and using asbestos for their production process, and the President could grant national-security exemptions of up to three years. It also directs the EPA to create public education materials about asbestos health risks and licensed removal services. Asbestos is a known cause of mesothelioma and other deadly cancers, and the bill's remaining legal uses had narrowed to a handful of industrial plants.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people exposed to asbestos: workers at the handful of plants still using it, household members exposed through their clothes, and anyone coming into contact with imported asbestos-containing products. A ban removes the last legal channels of exposure and, paired with the bill's public education requirement, better informs people about risks and licensed cleanup.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers and families exposed to asbestos

how_it_helps.text: One year after enactment, no person could manufacture, process, use, or sell in commerce commercial asbestos or any mixture or article containing it, eliminating the remaining legal routes of exposure.
The bill covers all eight commercial asbestos fiber types, including chrysotile, the only type still imported into the United States in significant quantities.

The EPA, with Health and Human Services, would have to build public education resources on asbestos health effects, federal prevention resources, and where to find licensed asbestos removal in each state.

In-place asbestos in buildings already installed is excluded from the distribution ban, and disposal of asbestos-containing material remains allowed, so the ban targets new commercial uses rather than forcing immediate removal from homes.

analysis.who_pays: The chlor-alkali industry, which used imported chrysotile asbestos to make the diaphragms in its chlorine production cells, would have to convert to asbestos-free or membrane technology within the two-year window. Any remaining importers or manufacturers of asbestos-containing products would lose their product lines, and those costs could flow partly into chlorine prices.

drawbacks.text: Chlorine plants that rely on asbestos diaphragms get only two years to convert; converting production cells is capital-intensive, and a rushed transition could raise costs or disrupt chlorine supply, which feeds water treatment and other essential uses.

The national security exemption lets the President authorize asbestos use for up to three years, extendable once to six, with the option to withhold publication of details from the public while informing only two congressional committees, a broad and weakly overseen carve-out.
The bill does nothing about asbestos already installed in buildings and products, so exposure from legacy asbestos, the largest source of risk, continues and remains governed by existing rules.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public health benefit is large and one-sided: asbestos causes fatal cancers with no known safe exposure level, and by 2023 its lawful American uses had narrowed to a small set of industrial applications with known alternatives. The main real cost, conversion expense for the chlorine plants, is acknowledged by the bill itself through its two-year carve-out, which weakens the ban's speed but makes the transition more workable. On balance a well-designed bill whose cost falls on a concentrated industry and whose benefit spreads across the population.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its environment subcommittee, and it never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Suzanne Bonamici introduced the bill on March 30, 2023, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
On April 7, 2023, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Environment, Manufacturing, and Critical Materials, and the record shows no further action of any kind for the rest of the Congress.
The bill ended with 37 cosponsors: 36 of 216 House Democrats and 1 of 224 House Republicans.

Under the bill's text, the ban would take effect one year after enactment, with an explicit two-year exception letting existing chlor-alkali facilities keep importing and using asbestos fibers for chlorine production diaphragms.
The Congress ended on January 3, 2025 with the bill still stuck in subcommittee, so the prohibition never became law and the statutory scheme it would have created never took effect.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The chlor-alkali producers and asbestos importers that would have faced the ban kept the existing rules, under which chrysotile asbestos could continue to be imported and used. Separately, the EPA later used its existing toxics authority to phase out some asbestos uses, but this bill's broader statutory ban never happened.

for.name: Suzanne Bonamici
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited cosponsors for a full commercial asbestos ban.

for.name: Asbestos Disease Awareness Organization
for.role: Victim and family advocacy group; the bill is named for Alan Reinstein, a mesothelioma victim whose widow founded the organization
for.what_they_did: Championed a full asbestos ban and the bill named for Reinstein.

against.name: Cathy McMorris Rodgers
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never brought it to a committee markup; it sat at the subcommittee level until the Congress ended.

against.name: Chlor-alkali chemical producers
against.what_they_did: Pressed regulators and Congress to preserve continued asbestos use for chlorine production and opposed a full ban.

sides.party_line_note: Support was almost entirely Democratic: 36 of 216 House Democrats cosponsored, versus 1 of 224 House Republicans, and with Republicans holding the committee chair, the bill never advanced.

industries.note: These plants were the main remaining users of imported chrysotile asbestos for production diaphragms; the ban plus a two-year carve-out would force them onto asbestos-free technology. Their interest in keeping cheap asbestos inputs runs against the public's interest in ending exposure.

industries.industry: Asbestos importers and makers of remaining asbestos-containing products
industries.note: One year after enactment they could no longer bring in or sell commercial asbestos or articles containing it, ending a product line whose profits depend on a known carcinogen.

industries.industry: Licensed asbestos abatement and remediation firms
industries.note: The bill requires public education materials pointing people to licensed mitigation services, and asbestos already in buildings stays subject to removal rules, sustaining demand for abatement work.
